title: Clear Creek County Wells: Depth, Yield and Cost
meta_description: Clear Creek County wells have a 252-foot median depth. Compare local yields, water levels and finished-well costs of about $22,400-$37,200.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Clear Creek County
intro_html:
A well budget in Clear Creek County starts with fractured rock, not a predictable layer of water-bearing sand. The median recorded depth is 252 feet, but the middle half of wells runs from 120 to 402 feet. That spread matters when pricing a lot in Floyd Hill, Upper Witter Gulch or St. Mary's.

Colorado DWR records contain 5,505 county well permits, with 3,504 recorded as constructed. These records give you a useful starting point—not a guarantee of depth, water supply or permitted uses on your parcel.

sections.heading: Why Clear Creek County Well Depths Vary So Much
sections.html:
In mountain granite and gneiss, a driller needs to intersect water-bearing fractures. Nearby holes can encounter very different fracture conditions. County permits overwhelmingly identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer; Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 0% of the records.

Among 3,454 wells reporting depth, the median is 252 feet and the middle half spans 120-402 feet. Treat that range as a reason to request a footage-based bid with clear charges for drilling deeper, rather than assuming the median will finish your well.

The 90th-percentile depth is 600 feet. Compare nearby completion records in Echo Hills or Pine Valley before using the county median as your parcel's budget depth.

sections.heading: A 7.0 GPM Median Does Not Guarantee Your Household Supply
sections.html:
The county's 1,646 reported pump yields have a 7.0 gpm median, with the middle half between 4.5 and 10.0 gpm. Most reported yields—65%—fall in the 5-15 gpm band. Those results are useful for initial planning, but a recorded yield is not a promise of sustained output today.

Only 1% report under 1 gpm, while 25% fall in the 1-5 gpm band. A buyer still needs to take low production seriously: household demand can arrive faster than a slow well replenishes its supply. Have the well's sustained production and recovery evaluated, then size pumping and storage around the results. Installing a larger pump does not make the fractures produce more water.

sections.heading: Water Levels Are Deeper Than Early Records, but Not Steadily Falling
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water inside a well—not the depth you must drill. Clear Creek County's median is 70 feet below ground, with a middle-half range of 30-120 feet. Only 204 records report this measurement, so coverage is much thinner than the depth data.

Decade medians move from 29 feet in the 1960s and 40 in the 1970s to 80 in both the 1980s and 1990s, then 100 in the 2010s and 80 in the 2020s. Later measurements are generally deeper than the early ones, but this is not a steady decline. Different wells and measurement conditions prevent treating these county summaries as a repeated measurement of one water table.

sections.heading: What the County's Permit and Driller History Tells You
sections.html:
Clear Creek County's largest listed permit decade is the 1990s, with 1,195 permits, followed by the 1970s with 1,115. Records show 419 in the 2010s and 181 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The latter is an incomplete decade, and permit issuance is not the same as completed drilling.

The most active driller entries are James Drilling Company (Keaton, Michael K.) with 452 records, Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert) with 325, and Walton with 288. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability or licensing. Domestic/household use accounts for 87% of permits, but each property's actual permit controls its allowed uses.

sections.heading: Budgeting a Bedrock Well Near Idaho Springs or Georgetown
sections.html:
The supplied cost model for fractured mountain bedrock uses $65-$100 per foot. At the county's 252-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $16,400-$25,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $22,400-$37,200.

Those are planning figures, not a parcel-specific quote. A lot near Idaho Springs or Georgetown needs its own assessment of rig access, drilling conditions and the route from the well to the house. Ask the contractor to spell out casing and grout allowances, pump equipment, trenching and electrical scope. Also establish what happens to the price if usable fractures are not found at the planned depth.

sections.heading: Mine Features, Water Testing and Low-Yield Risk
sections.html:
The environmental map identifies 3,790 historic mine features, 72 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 81 PFAS sampling/contamination sites within about 10 miles. These categories flag places to investigate; they do not establish that a particular well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location is not necessarily a confirmed contamination source.

Review nearby site information and obtain laboratory testing suited to the property's setting, including basic drinking-water testing and any additional contaminants identified by that review. Inspect casing, the well cap and surface drainage. The reported low-yield share does not measure dry-hole risk, so ask how unsuccessful drilling would be handled. Check septic feasibility and well separation requirements before committing to a house location.

sections.heading: Before Buying a Lot in Floyd Hill, Empire or St. Mary's
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit and well completion report, then compare nearby wells on the map. Records around Floyd Hill, Empire or St. Mary's are a better starting point for local questions than a countywide median alone, though neighboring fracture conditions can still differ.

Confirm that the permitted use matches your plans. An exempt household-use permit does not automatically authorize outdoor watering, and expanded uses may require additional water-rights review or augmentation. For an existing home, arrange water-quality and production testing before closing. For vacant land, coordinate the well location, septic area, driveway, rig access and building footprint before finalizing the site plan. Resolve water-supply uncertainty while you can still change the purchase terms.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Clear Creek County?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth is 252 feet, and the middle half ranges from 120 to 402 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 600 feet. These figures come from 3,454 depth reports. Fractured mountain bedrock makes individual results variable, so compare nearby completion records before setting a drilling budget.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Clear Creek County?
faq.a: The bedrock drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 252-foot median depth, the hole alone is about $16,400-$25,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $22,400-$37,200. Get a site-specific quote that addresses access, casing, grout and the cost of drilling beyond the planned depth.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Clear Creek County?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 7.0 gpm median, with the middle half between 4.5 and 10.0 gpm. Of the reported yields, 1% are under 1 gpm. Before buying, have sustained production and recovery evaluated rather than relying only on an old permit-record yield. Pump and storage choices should follow that assessment.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Clear Creek County?
faq.a: The supplied records cannot establish whether a specific well is safe. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 3,790 historic mine features, 72 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 81 PFAS sampling/contamination sites. Proximity alone does not prove contamination. Review nearby site findings and arrange laboratory testing appropriate to the property before drinking the water.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Clear Creek County?
faq.a: The decade medians do not show a steady drop. Static water depth increased from 29 feet in the 1960s to 100 feet in the 2010s, then measured 80 feet in the 2020s. Only 204 records report static levels, and these are not necessarily the same wells measured repeatedly. Property-specific measurements are more useful.
